hook.text: Every April, Thailand erupts into a nationwide water fight. Strangers soak each other with hoses and buckets.

buildup.text: Songkran marks the Thai New Year. Water symbolizes washing away the old year's bad luck.

discovery.text: Originally, water was gently poured over elders' hands as a sign of respect. The water fight came later.

twist.text: Tourism turned a gentle ritual into a massive party. Locals debate whether the chaos honors or erases tradition.

climax.text: Songkran shows how festivals evolve. Meaning layers on top of meaning across generations.

punchline.text: The water is the same. The reason keeps changing.

quiz.question: What does water symbolize during Songkran?

details.summary: Thailand's Songkran festival transforms the entire country into a massive water fight every April. Originally a gentle cleansing ritual marking the Thai New Year, it evolved into the world's largest water festival — three days of joyful combat where no one stays dry and everyone participates.
details.whyItMatters: Songkran shows how ancient New Year rituals can evolve into uniquely modern celebrations. Its global appeal demonstrates the universal human desire for communal, uninhibited joy.
takeaways: Songkran is the Thai New Year celebrated April 13-15
The water tradition evolved from gentle blessing to massive water fights
It is now one of the world's most popular festival tourist attractions

faq.question: How did Songkran become a water fight?
faq.answer: Traditionally, Songkran involved gently pouring scented water over elders' hands and Buddha images as a blessing. Over decades, the water element escalated — younger generations began splashing each other, then using water guns and hoses.

faq.question: Is the traditional Songkran still observed?
faq.answer: Yes. Alongside the water fights, Thais still visit temples, make merit, pour water on elders' hands, clean homes, and build sand pagodas. Many families observe the quiet, spiritual aspects before joining the public water celebrations.
